extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / educated early-18th-century public interested in manners, literature, and moral argument
extracted.subtask_description: Expository and satirical essays about taste, conduct, music, friendship, and public opinion as written for a periodical (The Spectator). Includes moral maxims, social prescriptions, and literary criticism aimed at shaping readers' behaviour and aesthetic judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Nature / apply talents to natural ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature does nothing in vain: the Creator...has appointed every thing to a certain Use and Purpose...Follow Nature (the Oracle of Delphos pronounced to Cicero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build upon nature as the foundation for conduct and art: choose pursuits aligned with one's natural genius. Examples: Cicero (Tully) fit for oratory, Virgil for poetry; planting 'upon Nature' leads to solid foundations and reduces impertinence. Anti-pattern: forcing oneself into roles unsuited to one's talents results in failure or ridicule (see Valerio, who had no genius for poetry yet persisted). The text treats opposition to nature as both folly and 'one of the most heinous Crimes'—a rebellion against Providence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation — do not excel in characters one is not fit for
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the Absurdity and Ridicule we meet with in the World, is generally owing to the impertinent Affectation of excelling in Characters Men are not fit for, and for which Nature never designed them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not covet attributes or roles beyond your natural bent. Examples/anti-patterns: 'Coxcombs' produced by misapplied talents; Valerio attempts poetry without genius producing insipid verse; Cælia (beauty but no wit) and Iras (wit but no beauty) each ruin their natural advantage by aspiring to the other's character; Semanthe alters her complexion and is distinguished as 'the Lady that paints so well.' Consequence: loss of real excellence and acquisition of ridiculous or bad qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graft upon Nature — assist, don't supplant, natural aptitude
rubrics_metrics.description: If Men would be content to graft upon Nature, and assist her Operations, what mighty Effects might we expect?...To build upon Nature, is laying the Foundation upon a Rock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate and amplify what nature gives rather than replace it. Practical implication for education and practice: encourage disciplines that extend innate bent; avoid trying to create excellence where the natural 'seeds' are absent (analogy with horticulture). Examples: Tully/Cicero and Virgil rewarded for following nature; trying to raise a jonquil without its seeds is futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacred music should be founded on inspired words and solemn diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Composers have one very great Incitement to it: They are sure to meet with Excellent Words...There is something so pathetick in this kind of Diction, that it often sets the Mind in a Flame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing church-music, use language drawn from scripture (Psalms, inspired writings) and employ Hebraic idioms where fitting, because these phrases enrich English with solemnity and force. Benefit: stronger devotional effect, purifying and exalting the passions, and producing lasting impressions greater than ordinary devotional language. Anti-pattern: choosing trivial or 'polite' diction unsuited to worship leaves prayers cold and dead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use music in worship to purify, exalt passions, and strengthen devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Musick, when thus applied, raises noble Hints in the Mind of the Hearer, and fills it with great Conceptions. It strengthens Devotion, and advances Praise into Rapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage composers and patrons to apply musical skill to sacred contexts (hymns, anthems) rather than only to stage entertainments. Historical claim: music among the chosen people was a religious art; drama originated from religious chorus. Practical outcome: worship that combines pleasure and duty, improving virtue as it raises delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: To understand public opinion, sample different social quarters
rubrics_metrics.description: When I consider this great City in its several Quarters and Divisions, I look upon it as an Aggregate of various Nations...I love to hear the Reflections that arise upon it in the several Districts and Parishes of London and Westminster, and to ramble up and down a whole Day together, in order to make my self acquainted with the Opinions of my Ingenious Countrymen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method for observation/reporting: visit multiple coffee-houses and districts because each has its own 'mouth' or local statesman and distinct interests—St. James's more political, Giles's different factional claims, Temple coffee-houses learned talkers, Cheapside practical merchants, Fish-street commercial concerns. The upper rooms often have more refined theorists; lower rooms give other perspectives. Use these localized voices to form a fuller picture of public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: People interpret events through self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: every one is apt to consider [news] with a Regard to his own particular Interest and Advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observing reactions to news, expect interpretation colored by personal stakes. Examples: merchant worrying about mackerel/pilchards when hearing of a foreign king's death; a haberdasher claiming prior knowledge to preserve reputation until contradicted by incoming letters. Use such examples as evidence of how private interest shapes public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about cross-sex friendships — platonic intimacy may become passion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Man's Heart has not the Abhorrence of any treacherous Design, he may easily improve Approbation into Kindness, and Kindness into Passion...the Friends of different Sexes very often find fatal Effects from their Unanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to avoid too-close platonic intimacy between opposite sexes if one wishes to preserve innocence and tranquility. The author confesses shunning agreeable women and expresses low opinion of 'Platonick Love' as it may swell into passion inconsistent with philosophy. Anti-pattern: friendships that conceal nothing and thereby produce jealousy, entanglement, or social disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public reparation must match the visibility of the offense
rubrics_metrics.description: unless you could contrive a way to make your Recantation as well known to the Publick, as they are already apprised of the manner with which you have treated me, you shall never more see Philander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social breaches of reputation (e.g., jilting), private apology may not suffice; public retraction or demonstration of repentance proportional to the publicness of the offense is necessary to restore trust. Example: Amoret is told her recantation must be made as public as her slight; otherwise reconciliation will not occur. Practical tactic: publish letters or make public amends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance solitude and public life — avoid extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Methinks most of the Philosophers and Moralists have run too much into Extreams, in praising entirely either Solitude or publick Life...Those who, like you, can make themselves useful to all States, should be like gentle Streams...but there is another sort of People who seem designed for Solitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribe a 'mixt State' between country solitude and civic life: too much rest makes one useless; too much public life destroys by precipitation. Some persons are naturally suited to solitude and should not be forced into continual public display. Use the metaphor of waters: gentle streams that visit towns but also glide through lonely vales are ideal. Practical implication: choose life arrangements fitting temperament and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and civic function of dramatic chorus — moral instruction via performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The first Original of the Drama was a Religious Worship consisting only of a Chorus...the Chorus so far remembered its first Office, as to brand every thing that was vicious, and recommend every thing that was laudable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using dramatic forms, retain their moral/religious function: performance should intercede for the innocent and implore vengeance on the criminal, thus serving as a civic moral instrument. Implication for playwrights/composers: art should promote virtue and admonish vice, not merely entertain.
